en: In the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: Uśan Vājaśravasa indeed gave away all his possessions.
He had a son named Naciketas. KaU 1.1.
While he was still a youth and the sacrificial gifts were being led away, faith entered him;
he reflected: (KaU 1.2)
Those who give such cows go to those worlds called "Joyless," where the water has been drunk, the grass eaten, the milk milked out, and the senses are gone. (KaU 1.3)
He said to his father, "Father, to whom will you give me? A second time and a third time he asked the same. He said to him, "I give you to Death. (KaU 1.4)
"I go as the first among many; I go as the middlemost among many.
What indeed is that duty of Yama which he will perform through me today? (KaU 1.5)
Observe how it was in the past, and observe likewise how it is for others;
like grain, a mortal ripens, and like grain, he is born again.
The Vaiśvānara fire enters the house as a Brāhmaṇa guest;
for him they perform this pacification: "O Vaivasvata, take water! (KaU 1.7)

Hope and expectation, social intercourse and pleasant speech, the merit of sacrifices and charitable works, as well as all sons and cattle—these are taken away from the man of small intelligence in whose house a Brahmin dwells without eating. (KaU 1.8)

"Since for three nights you have stayed in my house as a guest without eating, O Brahmin worthy of honor, let there be homage to you, O Brahmin, and may it be well with me; therefore, choose three boons in return. (KaU 1.9)
O Death, may Gautama be of tranquil resolve, well-disposed, and free from anger toward me; may he speak to me with a friendly mind when sent by you—this first of three boons I choose. (KaU 1.10)
As before, Auddālaki Āruṇi shall become confident, sent forth by me;
with his anger gone, he will sleep peacefully at night after seeing you released from the jaws of Death.

In the heavenly world there is no fear whatsoever; there you do not tremble at death nor at old age. Having crossed over both hunger and thirst, and having transcended sorrow, one rejoices in the heavenly world. (KaU 1.12)
O Death, you know that Agni who leads to heaven; tell it to me, for I have faith. Those who dwell in the heavenly world attain immortality—this I choose as my second boon. (KaU 1.13)

I shall declare this to you; listen well to it from me, O Naciketas, for I know that Agni who leads to heaven—know that he is the attainment of the infinite world and the final support, hidden within the secret cave of the heart. (KaU 1.14)
He told him about that Agni who is the beginning of the worlds—what bricks there are, how many, and how;
and he (the son) replied to that exactly as it was told. Then Death, being pleased, spoke to him again.
Being pleased, the Great-Souled One said to him: "I grant you yet another boon here today:
this fire shall be known by your very name; and take also this *sṛṅkā* of manifold forms. (KaU 1.16)
The one who has thrice kindled the Nāciketa fire, having attained the union by means of the three, and being a performer of the threefold duty, transcends birth and death.
Having known and realized the adorable God, born of Brahman, he attains this ultimate peace. (KaU 1.17)

O Triṇāciketa, having understood this triad, he who, knowing thus, builds the Nāciketa fire-altar, casts off the bonds of death before him and, transcending sorrow, rejoices in the heavenly world. (KaU 1.18)
This is that heavenly Agni Naciketas which you chose with your second boon.
People will call this very Agni yours; choose, O Naciketas, a third boon.
Regarding this doubt concerning a person after death—some say "it exists," and others say "it does not exist"—may I know this, instructed by you; this is the third of my boons. (KaU 1.20)
Even the gods had doubts about this in the past; for this Dharma is not easily understood, being so subtle.
Choose another boon, Naciketas; do not press me, let go of this one. (KaU 1.21)
Even the gods, it is said, were in doubt regarding this very matter, O Death, which you have declared to be so difficult to understand.
Another speaker like you cannot be found for this, nor is there anyone else who is equal to you as a boon.
Choose sons and grandsons who live for a hundred years, choose many cattle, elephants, gold, and horses; choose a vast expanse of land, and live yourself as many autumns as you desire. (KaU 1.23)
If you consider this equal [to the previous offer], choose a boon: wealth and long life;
O Naciketas, be a lord upon the great earth, and I shall make you a partaker of all desires. (KaU 1.24)
"Whatever desires are difficult to obtain in the world of mortals, ask for all those desires according to your wish!
These women, with their chariots and musical instruments—such as these are not to be obtained by men;
enjoy them with these who are given by me. O Naciketas, do not inquire about death. (KaU 1.25)
The morrow belongs to mortals, yet this end [of life] consumes the vigor of all the senses;
even the entirety of life is indeed short—your horses, your dancing, and your singing are for yourself alone. (KaU 1.26)
"A man cannot be satisfied with wealth; even if we were to obtain wealth, we would have seen you [already].
We shall live as long as you rule; however, that alone is the boon to be chosen by me. (KaU 1.27)

Having approached those who do not age and are immortal, what mortal standing below, subject to decay, knowing [this], could take delight—even while contemplating the excellence of colors, pleasures, and joys—in a life that is exceedingly long? KaU 1.28.
"O Death, tell us that about which they have doubts regarding the great hereafter;
this boon which has entered into the secret—other than that, Naciketas chooses nothing else. (KaU 1.29)
Thus ends the first chapter.
The good is one thing, and the pleasant is indeed another; these two, having different aims, bind a person.
Of these two, it is well for him who takes hold of the good; he who chooses the pleasant is deprived of his true purpose. (Katha Upaniṣad 2.1)
The wise man, having fully circled around both the beneficial and the pleasant, discriminates between them;
for the wise man chooses the beneficial over the pleasant, while the dull-witted chooses the pleasant for the sake of acquisition and security.
O Naciketas, you have renounced those desirable objects of pleasure and beautiful forms even while longing for them;
you have not attained this "hook" consisting of wealth, in which many men sink. (KaU 2.3)
Far apart and leading in opposite directions are these two, known as ignorance and knowledge.
I consider you, Naciketas, to be one who desires knowledge; many desires did not distract you. (KaU 2.4)
Existing in the midst of ignorance, yet considering themselves wise and learned, these deluded ones wander about, stumbling like blind men led by one who is himself blind. (KaU 2.5)
The world beyond does not reveal itself to the fool who is heedless, deluded by the infatuation for wealth;
thinking "this world exists, there is no other," he again and again falls under my sway. (KaU 2.6)

He who is not obtained even for hearing by many, and whom many, though hearing, do not know—he is a marvel as a speaker, skillful in its acquisition; he is a marvel as a knower, instructed by the skillful. (KaU 2.7)
This [Self], when taught by an inferior man, is not easily understood even though it is reflected upon in many ways;

there is no way to reach it if it is taught by anyone other than [the realized teacher], for it is subtler than the subtlest, being beyond the scope of logic and smaller than the smallest atom. (KaU 2.8)
This wisdom cannot be attained by mere reasoning; it must be taught by another who has realized it for the sake of right knowledge, O dearest one.
You have indeed attained it, for you are firm in truth; may you remain such as you are, O Naciketas, our most beloved.
"I know that which is called 'treasure' is impermanent; for the eternal is not attained by means of things that are non-eternal.
Therefore, the Nāciketa fire-altar was built by me, and through transient materials I have attained the Eternal. (KaU 2.10)
Having seen the attainment of desire, the foundation of the world, the infinity of sacrifice, and the further shore of fearlessness—
the great, wide-striding foundation of praise— the wise Naciketas, through steadfastness, has renounced them all.

Having realized through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self that ancient God—who is difficult to see, hidden, entered into the secret cave, seated in the abyss, and dwelling in the heart—the wise man casts off both joy and sorrow. (KaU 2.12)

Having heard this and having fully grasped it, a mortal who has extracted this subtle, righteous principle and attained it rejoices, for he has found that which is worthy of joy; I consider the abode to be opened for Naciketas.
Apart from dharma and apart from adharma, apart from what is done and what is not done,
and apart from what has been and what is to be— that which you see, tell me that.
That goal which all the Vedas proclaim, and which all austerities declare,
desiring which they lead the life of celibacy— that goal I tell you in brief.
"Om"—this is it. (KaU 2.15)
For this very syllable is Brahman; for this very syllable is the Supreme.
For having known this very syllable, whatever one desires becomes his.
This is the most excellent object of focus; this is the supreme object of focus.
Having known this object of focus, one is glorified in the world of Brahman.
The wise one is neither born nor does he die; this person has not come from anywhere, nor has he become anyone at all.
Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, he is not slain when the body is slain. (KaU 2.18)
If the slayer thinks to slay, or if the slain thinks himself slain, both of them do not understand; this one neither slays nor is slain. (KaU 2.19)
Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the secret cave of this living being.
Free from desire and with a serene mind, one beholds that majesty of the Self through the clarity of the elements.
Seated, he goes far; lying down, he goes everywhere.
Who other than me is able to know that God, who is beyond both intoxication and its absence? (KaU 2.21)
Having realized the Self— bodiless within bodies, stable within the unstable, great, and all-pervading— the wise man does not grieve.
This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing.
Only by whomsoever this [Self] chooses him is it attained; to him this Self reveals its own form. (KaU 2.23)

Neither one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not concentrated, nor even one whose mind is not at peace, can attain Him by means of wisdom. (KaU 2.24)
He for whom both the priesthood and the nobility are the rice, and for whom death is the condiment—who truly knows where he is? (KaU 2.25)
Thus ends the second Vallī.

Drinking the Truth (ṛta) in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest supreme realm, those who know Brahman—and those who have maintained the five sacred fires or the three Nāciketa rites—call them Shadow and Light. (KaU 3.1)
May we be able to attain the Nāciketa fire, which is the bridge for those who sacrifice, the imperishable Brahman that is supreme, and the fearless further shore for those desiring to cross over.
Know the self as the rider in the chariot, and the body indeed as the chariot;
know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins. (KaU 3.3)
The wise say that the senses are the horses and the sense-objects are their paths;
they say that the self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer. (KaU 3.4)
But for one who lacks discernment and whose mind is always undisciplined, the senses are uncontrollable, like the vicious horses of a charioteer. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.5)
But for one who possesses discernment and whose mind is ever disciplined, the senses are under control, like well-trained horses under a charioteer. (KaU 3.6)
But he who lacks understanding, who is without the mind, and is always impure,
does not attain that state and instead enters into the cycle of rebirth.
But he who possesses discernment, who is self-possessed and ever pure, attains that state from which he is not born again. (KaU 3.8)
But that man who has consciousness as his charioteer and holds the reins of the mind reaches the end of the journey— that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
For the objects are higher than the senses, and the mind is higher than the objects;
the intellect is higher than the mind, and the Great Self is higher than the intellect.
Greater than the Great is the Unmanifest; greater than the Unmanifest is the Person. There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal.
This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth;
yet it is seen by those who perceive the subtle with a sharp and subtle intellect. (KaU 3.12)
The wise man should restrain speech and mind; he should restrain them in the cognitive self (jñāna-ātman);
he should restrain the cognitive self in the Great Self (mahat-ātman), and he should restrain that in the Tranquil Self (śānta-ātman).
Arise, awake! Having reached the excellent [teachers], understand them.
The edge of a razor is sharp and difficult to traverse; that is what the seers call the path. KaU 3.14.

Having perceived that which is soundless, touchless, formless, imperishable, likewise tasteless, eternal, and odorless; which is without beginning or end, beyond the Great One, and immutable—one is released from the jaws of death. (KaU 3.15)
Having recited and heard this eternal narrative of Naciketas as proclaimed by Death, the wise man is glorified in the world of Brahman.
Whoever, being self-restrained, should proclaim this supreme secret in an assembly of Brahmins, or at the time of a funeral rite, that conduces to infinity;
it conduces to infinity. (KaU 3.17)
Thus ends the third chapter.
The Self-existent pierced the openings [of the senses] outward; therefore one looks outward, and not at the inner self.
But some wise man, desiring immortality, looked within the inward self with his gaze turned back. (KaU 4.1)
The foolish pursue outward desires; they go unto the snare of widespread death.
But the wise, having realized immortality, do not seek the permanent among the impermanent here on earth. (KaU 4.2)
By means of this very [consciousness], one discerns form, taste, smell, sounds, and tactile objects of sexual union; what remains here [to be known] beyond this?
This indeed is that. KaU 4.3.
The wise person does not grieve, having realized the great, all-pervading Self by which one perceives both the state of dream and the state of waking.
He who knows this eater of honey, the living self,
the lord of what has been and what is to be, does not shrink away from it.
This indeed is that. KaU 4.5.
He who was born before the heat, who was born before the waters,
and who, having entered the cave, beheld him as he stood there with all beings.
This indeed is that. KaU 4.6.
She who comes into being through the vital breath, Aditi, composed of the deities, who, having entered the secret cave, abides there and gave birth to all beings.
This indeed is that. KaU 4.7.
Jātavedas has been placed within the two kindling woods, well-nourished like an embryo by pregnant women; day after day Agni is to be praised by wakeful men who bring oblations.
This indeed is that. (KaU 4.8)
From which the sun rises and where it sets—into that all the gods are woven; no one transcends that.
This indeed is that. (KaU 4.9)
What is here is also there; what is there is also here.
He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity.
This must be attained by the mind alone; there is no diversity whatsoever here. He who perceives diversity here goes from death to death. (KaU 4.11)
The Person, the size of a thumb, dwells in the midst of the self;
he is the ruler of what has been and what is to be, and one does not shrink away from him.
This indeed is that. (KaU 4.12)
The Person, the size of a thumb, is like a smokeless flame;
he is the Lord of the past and the future; he alone is today, and he is tomorrow.
This indeed is that. KaU 4.13.
Just as water rained upon a mountain peak flows away in various directions,
so too one who perceives phenomena as separate runs after them alone.
Just as pure water poured into the pure becomes exactly like it, so does the self of the sage who understands become, O Gautama. KaU 4.15.
Thus ends the fourth Vallī.
Having ascended the eleven-gated city of the Unborn, whose mind is not crooked, one does not grieve; being liberated, he is set free.
This indeed is that. KaU 5.1.

The Swan dwelling in the pure, the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere, the Hotṛ-priest dwelling on the altar, the guest dwelling in the house, dwelling among men, dwelling in the best, dwelling in Truth, dwelling in the sky; born of the waters, born of the cows, born of Truth, born of the mountains—the Great Truth. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.2)
He leads the breath upward and casts the downward breath inward;
the All-Gods worship the Dwarf seated in the middle.
When this embodied being, whose body is falling apart and who is being released from the physical frame, what remains here?
This indeed is that. KaU 5.4.
No mortal lives by means of the out-breath (prāṇa) or the in-breath (apāna); rather, they live by something else upon which these two depend. (KaU 5.5)
Come now, I shall declare to you this secret, eternal Brahman,
and how the self becomes [transformed] upon reaching death, O Gautama.
Some embodied beings enter a womb for the sake of a body;
others pass into stationary objects, according to their karma and according to their knowledge.
This person who remains awake while others sleep, fashioning desire after desire—that indeed is the radiant, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal.
Upon it all worlds are supported; no one ever transcends it.
This indeed is that. KaU 5.8.

Just as fire, though one, having entered the world, assumes a form corresponding to every form, so too the single inner Self of all beings assumes a form corresponding to every form, both within and without. (KaU 5.9)

Just as the one wind, having entered the world, assumes a form corresponding to every form, so too the single inner self of all beings assumes a form corresponding to every form, both within and without. (KaU 5.10)

Just as the sun, the eye of the entire world, is not defiled by external ocular defects, so the one inner self of all beings is not defiled by the suffering of the world, being external to it. (KaU 5.11)
The one controller, the inner self of all beings, who makes his single form manifold—those wise ones who perceive him abiding within themselves attain eternal happiness, and no others. (KaU 5.12)

The eternal among the transient, the conscious among the conscious, the one who ordains the desires of the many—those wise ones who perceive Him abiding within themselves attain eternal peace, and no others. (KaU 5.13)
"This is it," they think, "the supreme bliss that cannot be described.
How indeed may I know it? Does it shine, or does it not shine? (KaU 5.14)

There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire. It is only by His shining that everything shines; by His light all this is illumined. (KaU 5.15)
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
With roots above and branches below, this is the eternal Ashvattha tree.
That indeed is the Radiant, that is Brahman, and that alone is called the Immortal.
Upon it all worlds are supported; no one transcends it.
This indeed is that. (KaU 6.1)
Whatever exists in this entire world, having issued forth, trembles in the vital breath;
it is a great terror, like a raised thunderbolt. Those who know this become immortal.
Out of fear of him the fire burns; out of fear the sun shines;
out of fear Indra and Vāyu, and Death as the fifth, run on.
If one is unable to realize this here before the dissolution of the body,
then one is subject to taking on a body again in the worlds of creation.
As it is in a mirror, so it is in the self; as it is in a dream, so it is in the world of the ancestors;
as one sees it clearly in water, so it is in the world of the Gandharvas; and as in shadow and sunlight, so it is in the world of Brahman.
Having understood the distinctness of the senses, as well as their arising and passing away as they emerge separately, the wise man does not grieve.

Higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect (sattva); higher than the intellect is the Great Self (mahān ātmā); and higher than the Great is the Unmanifest (avyakta). KaU 6.7.
But beyond the unmanifest is the Puruṣa, all-pervading and without marks;
by knowing him, a living being is liberated and attains immortality. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 6.8)
His form does not stand within the range of vision; no one sees him with the eye. He is conceived by the heart, by insight, and by the mind; those who know this become immortal. (KaU 6.9)
When the five senses, together with the mind,
come to rest and the intellect no longer stirs, they call that the supreme state.
They consider that steady control of the senses to be yoga; for at that time one becomes vigilant, since yoga is both the origin and the dissolution [of the senses]. (KaU 6.11)
It cannot be grasped by speech, nor by mind, nor by the eye;
how else can it be apprehended, other than by one who says, "It exists"? (KaU 6.12)
"It exists"—thus indeed should both be perceived by way of their true nature;
for one who perceives it as "it exists," the true nature becomes manifest.
When all desires that dwell within his heart are utterly released, then the mortal becomes immortal; even here he attains Brahman. (KaU 6.14)
When all the knots of the heart here are rent asunder, then the mortal becomes immortal; this indeed is the extent of the instruction. (KaU 6.15)
There are one hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head.
Going upward by that, one attains immortality; the others lead in various directions for departing [from the body].
The Person, the size of a thumb, is the inner self, eternally seated in the hearts of men.
One should draw him forth from one's own body with patience, as one extracts the stalk from the Muñja grass.
One should know him as the bright, the immortal—yes, one should know him as the bright, the immortal. (KaU 6.17)

Then Naciketas, having obtained this knowledge proclaimed by Death, as well as the entire method of yoga, attained Brahman, became free from passion, and was released from death; so too shall it be for another who knows the inner self (adhyātma) in this very way.
Thus ends the sixth chapter.
Thus ends the Kaṭha Upaniṣad.
